316.title: Exile
316.hook: since 1959 the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived in exile; a sorrow held with care
316.howItsDone: Tibetan communities in exile, centered on Dharamsala and settlements in India and Nepal, have re-founded major monasteries, schools and institutes, and many Tibetans mark March 10, the anniversary of the 1959 uprising, with prayers and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug, named and never ranked. Your line: four streams.

If you had one night to leave your home, and could never come back, what would you carry? Not what you'd pack. What you'd carry: the songs, the recipes, the prayers your grandmother said, the way your family does things. In 1959, and in the years after, a great many Tibetans faced some version of that question. Many of the practices you've met these two weeks, the chants, the mandalas, the teachers, reached the rest of the world because people carried them over the mountains.
screen: `ONE NIGHT TO LEAVE.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?` → `OVER THE MOUNTAINS, 1959.`

segments.voice: Here is the history, told plainly. Chinese forces entered Tibet, and in March 1959, after an uprising in Lhasa, the fourteenth Dalai Lama, still a young man, left the city at night. He crossed the Himalayas on horseback and on foot and reached India. Many Tibetans followed him, then and in the years after. India gave land and shelter, and the hill town of Dharamsala became the Dalai Lama's home and the seat of the Tibetan administration in exile. People hold strong and very different views about Tibet's politics, and the Chinese government describes these events very differently. This lesson stays with the people and the practice. Here is what they carried. Some texts came out on foot, in bundles. Others lived in the memories of monks, who recited them so they could be written down again. The great monasteries of Sera, Drepung and Ganden were founded anew in the fields of south India, and the debating courtyards filled with clapping and questions once more. Settlements grew in India and Nepal, and later in Europe and North America. Teachers who would never have left Tibet began teaching in cities all over the world. Tibetans speak of this loss with grief. The Dalai Lama has often said that those who drove them out are also to be held with compassion. That's the sorrow held with care: not pretending it didn't happen, not letting it turn into hatred. A tradition, carried on foot, into exile.

segments.voice: Picture Tibetans living far from the land their families came from, an old monk in south India, a teenager in a city apartment who has never seen Tibet, and silently offer them the metta phrases you learned: may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease. If you'd like, widen it to everyone, anywhere, who has had to leave home. Then rest in the breath.
Exile. Since 1959, the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived outside Tibet, carrying their practice with them: a sorrow held with care.
Your line: carried into exile. Grief, held with care and without hatred. That's day three hundred sixteen.

317.title: The bardo
317.hook: teachings on the in-between after death; a text read aloud to the dying
317.howItsDone: In Tibetan communities a lama or trained friend often reads the Bardo Thödol aloud beside the dying and, after death, beside the body, and families hold rituals during the forty-nine days that follow; many Theravada communities hold merit-making ceremonies for the dead instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: exile, a tradition carried over the mountains, a sorrow held with care. Your line: carried into exile.

A favorite song. A psalm. A letter from a grandchild. In hospice rooms, near the end, families sometimes read or play something to the one who is dying. Hospice staff are taught that hearing may be among the last senses to fade. Tibetan Buddhists have a whole text for that moment, read aloud beside the dying, and then beside the body for days afterward. It speaks directly to the one who has died, in a calm voice, telling them where they are.
screen: `A SONG, A PSALM, A LETTER.` → `HEARING, AMONG THE LAST TO FADE.` → `A TEXT READ ALOUD BESIDE THE DYING.`

segments.voice: Bardo is Tibetan for the in-between, a gap between one state and the next. Tibetan teachers describe several: the in-between of this life, of dreams, of meditation, of dying, and then, after death, the stages before a new birth. They teach that this last passage can last up to forty-nine days. First, they say, comes a moment of clear light, like a cloudless sky. If it isn't recognized, visions arise, peaceful and then fierce, and finally the mind is drawn toward a new life. The text that guides this is called, in Tibetan, Liberation Through Hearing in the In-Between. Tradition says Padmasambhava composed it and hid it, and that a treasure-finder named Karma Lingpa found it centuries later. In the West it's known as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, a title given by its first English editor. A lama or friend reads it near the one who has died, and its message, over and over, is simple: don't be afraid; these appearances are your own mind; recognize them, and be free. Buddhist traditions differ here. The Theravada Abhidhamma teaches that rebirth follows immediately, without an in-between, though some Theravada teachers allow for one. The Tibetan schools, and some other Mahayana traditions, teach the in-between in detail, and East Asian Buddhist rites also mark forty-nine days after a death. And Tibetan teachers add one more thing: every moment is a kind of bardo. Between jobs, between homes, between one breath and the next, things loosen, and change becomes possible. In between.

segments.voice: This one asks for a gentle heart, so go easy: if you're willing, let one thing come that you'd want read to you at the very end, a verse, a song, a few words from someone you love, without deciding anything. Then let it go, and rest in the small gap at the end of each out-breath, the tiny in-between before the next breath comes.
Bardo. The in-between: in Tibetan teaching, the passage between death and rebirth, and every gap where change becomes possible.
Your line: in between. Every moment, Tibetan teachers say, is a kind of bardo. Until tomorrow.

318.title: A Tibetan day
318.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often begin the day with water-bowl offerings and prostrations, circle temples and stupas clockwise with prayer beads, and shape each practice session with refuge and bodhicitta at the start and a dedication of merit at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bardo, the in-between after death, and in every gap of life. Your line: in between. Today, the last day of the diamond vehicle.

Early morning in a Tibetan settlement in India. A grandmother wakes before her family, washes her face, and fills seven small bowls with water on the family shrine. She lights a lamp and bows three times. Then she walks to the temple with her beads, joining a slow river of people circling it clockwise, murmuring, turning the prayer wheels as they pass. Later she'll sit for a while at home. None of it is dramatic. All of it has a shape.
screen: `SEVEN BOWLS OF WATER.` → `A LAMP, THREE BOWS.` → `CIRCLING THE TEMPLE WITH BEADS.`

segments.voice: Tibetan teachers often say a practice should be good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end. It begins with refuge: turning toward the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and in Tibetan practice often the teacher too. Right after comes bodhicitta, the reminder of why: for all beings. Many people say a short traditional verse joining the two, three times. The middle is the practice itself: om mani padme hum on the beads, a praise to Tara, a visualization, or tonglen, riding the breath. Whatever it is, teachers say to do it without grabbing at results. The end is dedication. Whatever good came from this is given away, to all beings, so it can't turn into a private trophy. A ten-minute session and a three-year retreat share that same shape. Around it sits the rest of the day: water bowls and lamps, the walk around the temple, the wheels, the flags on the roof. Now look back at two weeks on the roof of the world. The diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. Turn the mind. Check the teacher. Take in, send out. One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly. Swept away. Four streams. Carried into exile. In between. And today, the diamond day. Tomorrow the path comes down from the mountains, to wherever you live, with a practical question: who will you practice with?
screen: `BEGINNING: REFUGE AND BODHICITTA.` · `MIDDLE: MANTRA, TARA, TONGLEN.` · `END: GIVE THE GOOD AWAY.` · `WATER BOWLS, LAMPS, THE TEMPLE WALK.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape in miniature: begin by turning silently toward what you take refuge in, and remember you're not sitting only for yourself. In the middle, sit with the breath, or murmur om mani padme hum if that feels right, without chasing any result. At the end, give it away, whatever good came from this, for all beings; another day, the same shape can stretch to fifteen minutes.
A Tibetan day. Refuge and bodhicitta at the start, mantra or tonglen in the middle, and dedication at the end: good in the beginning, middle and end.
Your line: the diamond day. Good in the beginning, the middle and the end. Two weeks on the mountain, complete.

319.title: Finding a sangha
319.hook: temples, meditation centers, small groups: what to look for
319.howItsDone: Buddhists practice with a sangha at temples serving their communities, at meditation centers with weekly sits and retreats, and in small lay groups meeting in homes or online; many groups run on donations (dana).

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Tibetan day, good in the beginning, the middle and the end. Your line: the diamond day. And now, a new week.

For more than three hundred days, a lot of this path has happened between you and a screen. Early mornings, a bell, a breath. That counts. But the refuge itself makes a point about people. Of the three jewels, the Buddha, the teaching and the community, one is other people: people who sit when you don't feel like it, people who notice when you've gone missing. Today: finding a sangha.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED DAYS, MOSTLY ALONE.` → `THE THIRD JEWEL IS A COMMUNITY.` → `PEOPLE WHO NOTICE YOU'RE GONE.`

segments.voice: Sangha first meant the community of monks and nuns. Today many people also use it for any group who practice together, and it comes in a few shapes. First, temples. In many cities there are Thai, Sri Lankan, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Tibetan temples, built by communities who brought the teaching with them. Many welcome visitors, and some offer meditation classes in English. You may be the only newcomer in the room, and someone may hand you a plate of food. Second, meditation centers: insight, Zen, Tibetan, with a weekly sit, a talk, and sometimes retreats. Third, small groups: a handful of people in a living room, a library, a church basement, or online, sitting together on a Tuesday night. What should you look for? Teachers who are open about where their teaching comes from. Money that's explained; many groups run on dana, freely given. No pressure to commit, buy, or cut other ties. Room to ask questions. And one simple test: after a while, do the people who've been there longest seem kinder, calmer, more honest? That's the fruit. First visits are often awkward: you may not know when to bow, where to put your shoes, or what the chant is. That's normal. Try a place more than once before you decide, and it's fine to visit several. This week brings the admirable friend, warning signs, visiting a temple, and taking refuge. It starts here. You need people.

segments.voice: Wonder, without needing an answer yet, where people near you gather to practice: a temple, a center, a small group, even one that meets online. Then sit with the breath, and remember that somewhere, in a temple or a living room, others are sitting too.
Sangha. The community of practice: first the monastic order, now also any group, temple or circle where people sit together.
Your line: you need people. The third jewel is other people, and they're out there. Day three hundred nineteen.

320.title: The admirable friend
320.hook: Ananda says good friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha says it is the whole (SN 45.2)
320.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions treat the admirable friend, a teacher or a fellow practitioner, as central to practice, and many describe choosing good companions as part of the path itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sangha, the community of practice, the third jewel. Your line: you need people.

Half. That was Ananda's number. Tradition remembers him as the Buddha's cousin and, for many years, his attendant: the one who carried the bowl and remembered the talks. One day he came to the Buddha with something he had worked out about the spiritual life: how much of it rests on good friends. Half, he said. Good friendship is half of the holy life. It sounds like a generous answer. The Buddha didn't accept it.
screen: `ANANDA, THE ATTENDANT.` → `HOW MUCH RESTS ON GOOD FRIENDS?` → `HE SAID HALF.`

segments.voice: The scene is in a short discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya. Ananda says, in paraphrase: good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship, this is half of the holy life. And the Buddha answers: not so, Ananda. It is the whole of the holy life. Someone with admirable friends, he says, can be expected to develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path. Then he points to himself: it's by relying on him as an admirable friend that beings are freed from birth, aging and death. The Pali is kalyanamitta. Kalyana means good, beautiful, lovely. Mitta means friend, from the same family as metta, loving-kindness, the first word of this path. So an admirable friend isn't just a pleasant one. It's someone whose goodness rubs off on you. Elsewhere the Buddha says that when the mind isn't yet ripe, the very first thing that helps it ripen is an admirable friend. And in a long talk to a young householder, he describes the real friend: one who helps you when you're careless, who's the same in good times and bad, who points you toward what's good, and who is glad when you do well. So in this teaching, friendship isn't a nice extra beside the practice, something for weekends. It's the ground. Who you spend time with shapes what you think, what you laugh at, what you let slide. And it runs both ways: you can be that friend for someone. The whole of the path.

segments.voice: Name one admirable friend, someone whose goodness has rubbed off on you, alive or not, near or far; picture their face, remember one moment when they pointed you toward something good, and silently thank them. Then think of one person for whom you might be that friend. Let them both rest in your mind, and then rest in the breath.
Kalyanamitta. The admirable friend, whose goodness rubs off on you. Not half the holy life, the Buddha says: the whole of it.
Your line: the whole of the path. Not half, the Buddha said: all of it. Rest well, friend.

321.title: Cautions
321.hook: the Kalamas: test a teaching yourself, and trust no one who asks for secrecy or blind obedience (AN 3.65)
321.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Kalama Sutta to encourage students to test the teaching in their own experience, and many communities publish codes of conduct and financial information so that students can check a group openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalyanamitta, the admirable friend. Not half the holy life, the Buddha said, but the whole of it. Your line: the whole of the path.

You met the Kalamas back in the story camp. Their town, Kesaputta, was one teachers kept passing through. Each one, the sutta says, explained his own teaching and made it shine, and ran down everyone else's. Then the next one came and did the same. The Kalamas were left with a plain, tired question: which of these people is telling the truth? When the Buddha came through, they asked him exactly that. His answer is often quoted, and often quoted wrong.
screen: `TEACHERS KEEP PASSING THROUGH.` → `EACH ONE RUNS DOWN THE LAST.` → `WHICH OF THEM IS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha tells the Kalamas their doubt is reasonable. Then he gives a list, here in paraphrase. Don't go by reports, tradition or hearsay. Don't go by scripture, logic, inference, what merely seems plausible, or a view you already like. Don't go by how impressive a speaker is, or by the thought, this is our teacher. Instead, when you know for yourselves that certain things are unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when you act on them, let them go. When you know things are wholesome, praised by the wise, and lead to well-being, take them up. Then he asks them: does greed lead to benefit or harm? Hatred? Delusion? And they answer for themselves. Notice what the sutta does not say. It isn't believe whatever feels right. It points to results you can watch in your own life, and to the judgment of wise people. There's a second caution, and it comes from other texts, not this one. In a short discourse the Buddha says the sun, the moon and his teaching shine openly; they aren't hidden. And near the end of his life he said he had never held back anything in a closed fist. Some traditions keep certain practices for students who have prepared, as you saw in the Tibetan weeks. That's different from secrecy about money, or about how people are treated, or demands for obedience that override your conscience. Those are warning signs anywhere. Test it yourself.
screen: `YOUR DOUBT IS REASONABLE.` · `KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.` · `WATCH THE RESULTS, ASK THE WISE.` · `THE TEACHING SHINES OPENLY.` · then, large: `TEST IT YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Pick one warning sign you'd want to remember in any group, spiritual or not: being told not to ask questions, money nobody explains, being pulled away from friends. Then sit with the breath and test something right now: does this breath, watched closely, bring agitation or ease? Just look.
Cautions. The Buddha told the Kalamas to know for themselves, by results and by the wise, and his teaching shines openly, not in secret.
Your line: test it yourself. Your doubt, the Buddha said, is reasonable. That's three hundred twenty-one days.

322.title: Visiting a temple
322.hook: shoes off, bow, sit toward the back, don't point your feet at the shrine
322.howItsDone: Visitors to Buddhist temples usually remove their shoes, dress modestly, bow or join their palms, sit toward the back and keep their feet from pointing at the shrine or monks; in many Theravada temples women do not hand things directly to monks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Kalamas, told to know for themselves, by results and by the wise. Your line: test it yourself. Today closes the week.

You're standing at the gate of a temple for the first time. There's a pile of shoes by the steps. Inside, a soft chant, and the smell of incense. Someone walks past you and bows. First-time visitors tend to carry the questions of a guest at a stranger's wedding: am I dressed right, where do I stand, what if I do it wrong? A handful of customs covers most of it, and a guest who's trying is usually met kindly.
screen: `A PILE OF SHOES BY THE STEPS.` → `CHANTING, INCENSE, A BOW.` → `WHAT IF I DO IT WRONG?`

segments.voice: Shoes off. At the door of the shrine hall, and in some countries at the gate of the whole temple, shoes come off; look for the pile and add yours. Dress simply, with shoulders and knees covered. Inside, many Buddhists bow three times, the three bows from your very first week, to the Buddha, the teaching and the community. In Theravada temples it's often a five-point bow: forehead, forearms and knees to the floor. As a guest, you can simply put your palms together at your chest and lower your head a little. That gesture is anjali; in Thailand it's the wai. Sit toward the back, on the floor or a chair, whatever others are doing. And the custom that's easiest to miss: don't point your feet at the Buddha image, the shrine, or a monk. In much of Asia the feet are the lowest part of the body, so pointing them is like pointing a dirty shoe. Sit cross-legged, or fold your legs to the side. A few more. In many Theravada temples, women don't touch monks or hand them things directly; an offering is placed on a cloth or passed through someone else. Walk clockwise around a stupa. Ask before taking photos. Don't touch or climb on images. Customs differ between a Thai temple, a Japanese one and a Tibetan one; when in doubt, watch and copy, or ask. Now look back at the week. Carried into exile. In between. The diamond day. You need people. The whole of the path. Test it yourself. And today: shoes off.
screen: `SHOES OFF, SHOULDERS COVERED.` · `THREE BOWS, OR PALMS TOGETHER.` · `SIT BACK, FEET AWAY FROM THE SHRINE.` · `WATCH, COPY, ASK.` · then, large: `SHOES OFF.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself at a temple gate, even for a visit months away: shoes off, palms together, a seat toward the back, feet tucked away from the shrine. Notice how the nerves feel, and let them be. Then sit here the way you'd sit there: quietly, a guest in a room full of other people's devotion.
Anjali. The gesture of palms joined at the chest, a greeting and a sign of respect used when entering a shrine hall.
Your line: shoes off. A handful of customs, and a guest who's trying. A week done; see you tomorrow.

chat.meaning: In much of Asia the feet are the lowest part of the body, so pointing them at the image, shrine or a monk is rude.
